mcq.section: Classes for Java and Python refugees
mcq.prompt: In `Order order{"EURUSD", 200};`, what does the variable `order` hold?
choices: The Order object itself
A pointer to an Order, implicitly dereferenced
A handle managed by the runtime
A reference to an Order allocated elsewhere
mcq.explain: A C++ variable of class type normally contains the object. This is the first thing to unlearn coming from Java or Python: the declaration chooses between value, pointer and reference, rather than every class variable being reference-like.

mcq.section: Classes for Java and Python refugees
mcq.prompt: What is the only difference between `class` and `struct` in C++?
choices: struct cannot participate in inheritance
Default member access (and default inheritance access)
struct objects are always trivially copyable
struct cannot have member functions
mcq.explain: class members are private by default, struct members public by default; otherwise they have identical capabilities. The convention — struct for passive data whose fields are independently valid, class when an invariant must hold — is a convention, not a language rule.

mcq.section: Classes for Java and Python refugees
mcq.prompt: What does the trailing const in `std::int64_t quantity() const;` qualify?
choices: Every parameter of the function
The return value, making it non-assignable
The object observed through this
The function, preventing it from being overridden
mcq.explain: It makes this a pointer to const, so the function may be called through a const Order& and cannot modify ordinary data members. A non-const member function requires a non-const object — which is why `snapshot.add_quantity(10)` on a const reference fails to compile.

mcq.section: Invariants and access control
mcq.prompt: What is an invariant, in the sense this chapter uses the word?
choices: A compile-time constant belonging to the class
A field that no member function writes to
A member declared const
A condition that holds after construction and after every public operation
mcq.explain: The point of encapsulation is to put every state-changing path behind one boundary so that illegal states are unrepresentable outside it. If every private field has an unrestricted setter, the type is a public struct wearing access labels.

mcq.section: Invariants and access control
mcq.prompt: A `friend` declaration inside a class does what?
choices: Grants the named non-member function access to private state
Makes the class's private members public to the enclosing namespace
Inherits the friend's interface into the class
Makes the named function a member of the class
mcq.explain: friend grants access; it does not confer membership. A hidden friend — defined inside the class — is invisible to ordinary namespace lookup and found only by ADL on its arguments, which keeps it out of unrelated overload sets.

mcq.section: Constructors, destructors, and member initializer lists
mcq.prompt: In what order are data members initialised?
choices: In the order they appear in the member initializer list
In declaration order within the class
Alphabetically, so the order is deterministic
Unspecified — the compiler may choose
mcq.explain: Declaration order is construction order, and the written order of the initializer list is ignored for this purpose (-Wreorder warns when they disagree). Destruction is the exact reverse. Treat -Wreorder as a correctness warning: a member initialised from a not-yet-initialised sibling reads indeterminate storage.

mcq.section: Constructors, destructors, and member initializer lists
mcq.prompt: Why prefer a member initializer list over assignment in the constructor body?
choices: It allows members to be initialised out of declaration order
Purely stylistic — the generated code is identical
It initialises directly instead of default-constructing then assigning, and it is the only way to set const and reference members
It runs before the base class is constructed
mcq.explain: Assignment in the body first default-constructs the member (an empty std::string, say) and then overwrites it. const and reference members cannot be assigned at all, so they must be bound in the initializer list.

mcq.section: Constructors, destructors, and member initializer lists
mcq.prompt: What does declaring any constructor do to the implicit default constructor?
choices: It suppresses the implicit copy constructor as well
It makes the default constructor deleted but still declared
Nothing — the default constructor is always generated
It suppresses the implicit default constructor
mcq.explain: A user-declared ordinary constructor removes only the implicit default constructor. Copy and move operations survive. If the type also needs `T{}`, declare it deliberately — and make it choose a valid state.

mcq.section: Special member functions and the rules
mcq.prompt: A class declares `~T() = default;` and nothing else. Which operations does the compiler still implicitly declare?
choices: Default ctor and both copies (the copies deprecated); no implicit moves
Default ctor only
Both moves but not the copies
All five others: default ctor, both copies, both moves
mcq.explain: = default still counts as a user declaration. A declared destructor leaves the copy operations implicitly generated but deprecated, and suppresses both implicit moves. This is the trap behind 'adding a logging destructor made my container slow': relocation falls back to copying.

mcq.section: Special member functions and the rules
mcq.prompt: A class declares a move constructor and nothing else. What is the status of its copy constructor?
choices: Deprecated but generated
Defined as deleted
Not declared at all
Implicitly generated
mcq.explain: Declaring a move operation causes the implicit copies to be defined as deleted. Deleted is not the same as absent: overload resolution still finds the function, and selecting it is a compile error rather than a silent fallback to something else.

mcq.section: Special member functions and the rules
mcq.prompt: What is the rule of zero?
choices: Give every class a zero-argument constructor
Declare all five special members as = default
Declare none of the copy, move or destruction operations, letting members manage their own behaviour
Use zero-initialisation for every member
mcq.explain: If std::string and Price already know how to copy, move and destroy themselves, the compiler-generated operations do the right thing member-wise. Rules of three and five apply only once the class itself owns a resource — and then you declare the whole set, so a later reader does not have to reconstruct the suppression matrix.

mcq.section: Special member functions and the rules
mcq.prompt: Why declare `void set_quantity(double) = delete;` alongside `void set_quantity(std::int64_t);`?
choices: To force the double to be truncated at the call site
To make the integer overload a better match
To document that doubles are not supported, with no effect on compilation
Because a deleted overload still participates in overload resolution, so a double argument selects it and fails instead of silently converting
mcq.explain: Deleted functions are declared, so they compete normally. set_quantity(250.5) picks the exact deleted match and errors, rather than quietly converting to 250. This is a general technique for closing off unwanted conversions.

mcq.section: Converting and explicit constructors
mcq.prompt: `void submit(Order);` where Order has a non-explicit `Order(std::int64_t)`. What does `submit(42)` do?
choices: Constructs an Order implicitly from 42 and calls submit(Order)
Calls submit with an uninitialised Order
Is ambiguous
Fails to compile — no submit(int) overload exists
mcq.explain: A constructor callable with one argument defines a user-defined conversion, which overload resolution will apply. The source reads as though it submits an integer. Mark single-argument constructors explicit by default; omit it only for a natural, lossless, unsurprising conversion.

mcq.section: Converting and explicit constructors
mcq.prompt: With `explicit SafeOrder(std::int64_t)`, which line still compiles?
choices: SafeOrder order = 42;
SafeOrder order{42};
None of them
submit(42);
mcq.explain: explicit removes the constructor from copy-initialisation and from implicit conversion during overload resolution, but direct construction with braces or parentheses is exactly how you spell the conversion when you mean it.

mcq.section: Converting and explicit constructors
mcq.prompt: Why is `explicit operator bool() const` usually the right spelling for a conversion operator?
choices: Because bool cannot be returned from a non-explicit operator
Because implicit conversion operators are ill-formed in C++23
Because it still works in a condition, while blocking broad implicit conversion to integer types
Because explicit conversion operators are cheaper at runtime
mcq.explain: Conditions are a contextual-conversion context, so `if (status)` works even for an explicit operator bool. Without explicit, the type would also convert to int and participate in arithmetic and comparisons that make no sense for it.

mcq.section: Delegating and inherited constructors, statics, and ref-qualifiers
mcq.prompt: What is true of a delegating constructor?
choices: It must delegate to a base-class constructor
It runs before the target constructor
It may also have its own member initializer list
Only the target constructor initialises members; the delegating body may add work afterwards
mcq.explain: The delegation replaces the member initializer list entirely — you cannot delegate and also initialise members directly. The delegating constructor's body runs after the target completes, which is where any extra setup goes.

mcq.section: Delegating and inherited constructors, statics, and ref-qualifiers
mcq.prompt: What do the ref-qualifiers in `Order build() &&;` and `Order build() & = delete;` accomplish?
choices: They restrict the value category of the object the function may be called on
They control whether the return value is moved or copied
They mark the function as taking an rvalue parameter
They are required for any function returning by value
mcq.explain: Ref-qualifiers apply Chapter 3's value categories to the implicit object. Only an rvalue OrderBuilder can be built from, so `OrderBuilder{250}.build()` compiles and `builder.build()` on a named object does not — communicating that building consumes the builder's logical state.

mcq.section: Delegating and inherited constructors, statics, and ref-qualifiers
mcq.prompt: What can a static member function access directly?
choices: Only members declared inline static
Only static members — it has no this pointer
All members, through an implicit this
Only public members
mcq.explain: A static member function belongs to the class, not to an object, so there is no this. `inline static` (C++17) is the companion feature that lets a static data member be defined inside the class rather than needing a separate out-of-line definition.

mcq.section: Bit-fields
mcq.prompt: Which operation is ill-formed on a bit-field member?
choices: Assigning to it
Reading it
Taking its address
Comparing it
mcq.explain: A bit-field has no addressable storage of its own, so neither `&flags.urgent` nor a reference to it is allowed. Adjacent nonzero-width bit-fields also normally share one memory location, which matters for data races (Chapter 25).

mcq.section: Bit-fields
mcq.prompt: Why should a wire format use explicit shifts and masks rather than a bit-field struct?
choices: Bit-fields cannot use unsigned base types
static_assert cannot be applied to bit-field structs
Bit-fields are slower to read
Bit-field allocation order and straddling rules are implementation-defined, so bit positions are not portable
mcq.explain: Allocation may proceed from low to high bits or the reverse, and whether a field may straddle an allocation unit is up to the implementation. static_assert(sizeof(MsgFlags) == 2) checks the size, not the bit positions. Bit-fields are for internal packing under a fixed ABI.

mcq.section: Inheritance and composition
mcq.prompt: In what order do construction and destruction proceed for a derived object?
choices: Base constructor then derived; derived destructor then base
Base constructor then derived; base destructor then derived
Unspecified
Derived constructor then base; base destructor then derived
mcq.explain: Construction starts with the base subobject, then derived members, then the derived constructor body. Destruction mirrors it exactly — derived body first, then derived members, then the base subobject.

mcq.section: Inheritance and composition
mcq.prompt: What does private inheritance express?
choices: is-a, with the base interface hidden from callers
implemented-in-terms-of: no base conversion is available to outside code
The base's private members become accessible to the derived class
The derived class cannot be inherited from further
mcq.explain: Under private inheritance the base's public names are inaccessible outside and no implicit derived-to-base conversion is available to callers. It is rare — a member of the policy type usually communicates the same relationship more directly.

mcq.section: Object slicing
mcq.prompt: `std::vector<Order> orders; orders.push_back(limitOrder);` — what is stored?
choices: A reference to the original LimitOrder
A copy of the LimitOrder, with its dynamic type preserved
An Order constructed from the Order subobject; the derived members are sliced away
The code fails to compile
mcq.explain: The vector's slots are exactly sizeof(Order); there is nowhere to put limit_, and the new object's runtime type is Order — so even a virtual kind() returns "Order". This is where Java or Python reference intuition fails: the container stores values.

mcq.section: Object slicing
mcq.prompt: Which of these does NOT prevent slicing?
choices: Storing pointers to polymorphic objects instead of values
Making the polymorphic base abstract
Keeping a homogeneous value container and not using inheritance for its elements
Making the base destructor virtual
mcq.explain: A virtual destructor fixes deletion through a base pointer, an entirely different bug. Slicing is a copy-construction problem: making the base abstract is what makes constructing a base value ill-formed and thus catches it at compile time.

mcq.section: Virtual functions, vtables, and abstract classes
mcq.prompt: Which is the larger cost of virtual dispatch in typical hot code?
choices: The lost inlining, which blocks constant propagation and register scheduling across the boundary
The RTTI metadata added to the binary
The extra pointer of storage per object
The two dependent loads and the indirect call instruction
mcq.explain: The dispatch instructions themselves are cheap. An unresolved indirect call prevents the optimiser from seeing into the callee at all — no constant exposure, no branch removal, no keeping intermediates in registers. That is usually what shows up in a profile.

mcq.section: Virtual functions, vtables, and abstract classes
mcq.prompt: A base constructor calls a virtual function that the derived class overrides. Which body runs?
choices: The derived override, as with any virtual call
The base version — the derived part is not alive yet
It is undefined behaviour
The program fails to compile
mcq.explain: While the base subobject is being constructed, the active runtime type is the base; dispatch does not reach a more-derived part that is not yet alive. The mirror restriction applies during base destruction. Calling a virtual hook from a constructor expecting derived behaviour is the bug.

mcq.section: Virtual destructors and deleting through base pointers
mcq.prompt: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is:
choices: Implementation-defined
Well-defined — only the base destructor runs
Undefined behaviour
A compile error
mcq.explain: 'Only the base destructor runs' is a common symptom, not the rule. The behaviour is undefined: the implementation may also use the wrong deallocation size, or optimise on the assumption that the execution never happens. Sanitizers catch some instances, not all.

mcq.section: Virtual destructors and deleting through base pointers
mcq.prompt: What does a protected non-virtual destructor on a polymorphic base express?
choices: That derived classes must declare their own virtual destructor
That the class is abstract
That the base may only be destroyed by friends
A non-owning callback interface: calls are allowed, deletion through the base is a compile error
mcq.explain: It is the other half of the rule: a polymorphic base is either publicly destructible through a virtual destructor, or not publicly destructible through the base at all. The protected form permits `listener->on_message()` while making `delete listener` fail to compile.

mcq.section: `override`, `final`, and covariant returns
mcq.prompt: A derived class declares `void handle(long) const` where the base has `virtual void handle(int) const`. Without `override`, what happens?
choices: It silently declares a different function; calls through a base reference reach the base version
The program is ill-formed
It overrides, but only for long arguments
It overrides the base function — long and int are compatible
mcq.explain: An override must match the signature exactly, including parameter types and member qualifiers. A near-miss quietly becomes a new function that hides nothing and overrides nothing. Writing `override` turns that silent drift into a compile error — and do not also repeat `virtual`.

mcq.section: `override`, `final`, and covariant returns
mcq.prompt: A derived class declares `void parse(const std::string&)` while the base has `parse(int)` and `parse(double)`. What does `derived.parse(7)` do?
choices: Calls Parser::parse(int)
Fails: the derived declaration hides all base overloads of that name
Calls the derived parse with 7 converted to a string
Is ambiguous between the three candidates
mcq.explain: Name lookup stops at the first scope containing the name, so the derived declaration hides the entire base overload set — even signatures it does not override. `using Parser::parse;` in the derived class re-exposes them.

mcq.section: Multiple inheritance, virtual inheritance, and RTTI
mcq.prompt: In a non-virtual diamond, why is `order.id` ambiguous?
choices: Because virtual inheritance is required for any multiple inheritance
Because the two intermediate bases declare conflicting members
Because the derived object contains two separate Identity subobjects
Because id is private in one path
mcq.explain: Each non-virtual base contributes its own subobject, so RoutedOrder holds two Identity::id fields and the unqualified name cannot pick one — you must write order.VenueIdentity::id. Virtual inheritance requests a single shared top-base subobject instead, at the cost of runtime-adjusted offsets.

mcq.section: Multiple inheritance, virtual inheritance, and RTTI
mcq.prompt: What does `typeid(a) == typeid(b)` compare?
choices: Whether the two objects have the same size and layout
Whether both are polymorphic
Whether a's type derives from b's type
Exact runtime types
mcq.explain: typeid equality is exact-type equality; it never answers the derives-from question — that is dynamic_cast's job. And dynamic_cast is not one tag comparison: it may query a runtime type graph and adjust a pointer across a multiple-inheritance hierarchy.

mcq.section: CRTP and type erasure
mcq.prompt: What can CRTP NOT do that a virtual base can?
choices: Hold several derived types in one heterogeneous runtime container
Access members of the derived class
Avoid a per-object vptr
Inline the dispatched call
mcq.explain: FeedBase<SimFeed> and FeedBase<LiveFeed> are unrelated types — there is no common runtime base to point at. CRTP trades runtime flexibility for compile-time coupling and generates code per specialisation; type erasure is what recovers a heterogeneous container without an intrusive base.

mcq.section: CRTP and type erasure
mcq.prompt: Does type erasure remove virtual dispatch?
choices: Yes — that is the point of the technique
No: this implementation hides a private vtable behind a value interface; the win is decoupling and uniform storage
Only when the stored type is trivially copyable
Only in builds compiled with -fno-rtti
mcq.explain: Poller pays an indirect call plus, in this sketch, a heap allocation per model. What it buys is that the stored types need not inherit from anything. Construct erased wrappers outside per-message paths and keep them long-lived.

reading.section: Constructors, destructors, and member initializer lists
reading.explain: Two orderings collide here. Members are initialized in *declaration* order regardless of how the initializer list is written, so `a_` runs before `b_` and the output starts `AB`, not `BA`. Then the target constructor of the delegation finishes its body (`T`) before control returns to the delegating constructor, whose body runs last (`D`). The tempting reading is `BATD` — following the written initializer list — or `DBAT`, from expecting the delegating constructor to be the outer wrapper that runs first. A delegating constructor is not a caller-first wrapper: the target fully constructs the object, then the delegating body executes.

Assigning through a base reference calls `Shape::operator=(const Shape&)`, which copies only the `Shape` subobject of `square`. The object `shape` keeps its own identity and runtime type, so every call on it dispatches to `Shape::sides` and prints 0; only the call through `pointer`, which really addresses a `Square`, prints 4. The tempting reading is `440`, or `444`, from expecting assignment to replace the object the way rebinding a Python name would. Assignment writes into an existing object of a fixed type — it cannot change what that object is.

reading.section: Virtual functions, vtables, and abstract classes
reading.explain: While a base constructor runs, the object is only a `Stage`, so the virtual call in `Stage::Stage` reaches `Stage::announce`; the `Compress` constructor body then runs with the object complete and reaches `Compress::announce`. Destruction mirrors it: `~Compress` runs first while the object is still a `Compress`, then `~Stage` runs after the derived part has been destroyed and dispatches to `Stage::announce`. The tempting reading is `compress compress compress compress`, since `announce` is virtual and the object "is" a `Compress` throughout. During construction and destruction the dynamic type is whichever part is currently alive — which is exactly why virtual hooks called from constructors never reach derived state.

reading.prompt: Which of the three numbered lines compile, and which do not?
reading.explain: Only (1) compiles. `explicit` removes the constructor from consideration in copy-initialization, so (2) fails even though it looks like an ordinary initialization, and it removes the user-defined conversion from overload resolution, so (3) fails with no viable `sleep_for`. The tempting reading is that `explicit` bans only the `= ` form and that a function call still converts, or that `Millis timeout = 250;` is fine because the type is spelled on the left. Both (2) and (3) are copy-initializations of a `Millis` from a `long`; direct-initialization with braces or parentheses is what the keyword requires.

reading.prompt: A line-oriented buffer adds a single-character overload. Which call fails, and what makes the *other* call the more dangerous one?
reading.explain: The derived `append` hides *every* base overload, so `Buffer::append(const char*)` is not even a candidate: name lookup stops at `LineBuffer`, and a `const char*` does not convert to `char`, so the second call fails to compile. The tempting reading is that overloads accumulate across the inheritance boundary the way they do within one class. The failure is the lucky case: `buffer.append(65)` also stops at `LineBuffer`, but `int` to `char` is a valid conversion, so it silently calls the single-character overload instead of `Buffer::append(int)`. `using Buffer::append;` in `LineBuffer` re-exposes the inherited set and fixes both.

reading.section: Multiple inheritance, virtual inheritance, and RTTI
reading.explain: This is a cross-cast: `dynamic_cast` walks the runtime type graph of the complete object, finds that the `Drawable` really is a `Button`, and returns the address of its `Clickable` subobject — so the cast succeeds. That subobject is a *different* subobject with its own vptr, so the two pointers cannot compare equal even though they belong to one object; `dynamic_cast` adjusted the address. `typeid` on a polymorphic lvalue reports the complete runtime type, which is `Button`. The tempting reading is `true true true`, from the assumption that a pointer to an object is one address; under multiple inheritance a pointer carries which subobject it names as well as where it is.

reading.prompt: Why does this not compile, and which line does the compiler actually reject?
reading.explain: `final` on a class forbids derivation, so the rejected construct is the base-clause of `Base64Url` — `cannot derive from final base class` — and the `override` inside it is a second, dependent error. The tempting reading is that `final` only forbids further *overriding* of virtual functions, so `Base64Url` would be legal as long as it did not touch `encode`; that is what `final` means when written on a member function, not on a class. Class-level `final` is a promise to the optimizer as much as to the reader: it is what lets a call through a `Base64` reference be devirtualized.

The override returns `Leaf*` where the base returns `Node*`, which is a covariant return: legal because `Leaf*` converts to `Node*`. Calling `clone()` on an expression of static type `Leaf` therefore yields a `Leaf*` with no cast at the call site, while calling through `Node*` dispatches to the same override and yields the same object viewed as `Node*`. Both print `leaf`. The tempting reading is that `through_base` prints `node`, because the static type of the *pointer* is `Node*` — the return type is chosen from the static type of the call, but which function runs is chosen from the runtime type of the object.

reading.prompt: This registry stores base *pointers* precisely to avoid slicing its listeners. What has it bought instead?
reading.explain: Storing pointers does avoid slicing — the dynamic type survives — but a pointer neither owns nor extends anything. Each `ConsoleListener` is destroyed at the end of its loop iteration, so both entries in `registry` dangle before the second loop starts, and the virtual call loads a vptr out of dead stack: undefined behaviour, reported by ASan as `stack-use-after-scope`. The tempting reading is that the two calls print 0 and 1 because the storage "is still there" and nothing has overwritten it; that describes one run of one build, and the compiler is entitled to reuse that storage for the next iteration. Both objects must outlive the registry — a longer-lived owner, or the ownership types of Chapter 8.

The base knows its own derived type as a template argument, so `static_cast<const Derived&>(*this)` is a compile-time downcast and both `factor()` and `raw()` are resolved statically — no vptr, no virtual dispatch, and `twice()` can even return `Derived` by value, which a runtime-polymorphic base could never do. The tempting reading is that the `static_cast` is the unchecked downcast the chapter warns about; here it is safe precisely because the class *is* the template argument, and it would be undefined only if some class inherited `Unit<Feet>` without being `Feet`. Note the price: `Unit<Feet>` and `Unit<Metres>` are unrelated types, so no container can hold both.

writing.prompt: Write a `RetryBudget` class whose invariant is 0 <= used <= limit, established at construction and preserved by every public operation. It needs: an explicit constructor taking the limit and rejecting a negative one; `consume()` returning `false` instead of exceeding the limit; `reset()`; a `remaining()` observer; and a hidden-friend stream inserter printing used/limit. No caller may be able to set `used` directly.
checklist: Both data members are private and there is no setter for the used count
The constructor is `explicit` and rejects an invalid limit before the object becomes usable
`consume()` checks the limit before incrementing and reports failure by return value
The observers are `const` member functions
The stream inserter is a `friend` defined inside the class body
writing.notes: The test to reach for is whether a caller can write a line that breaks the invariant. A `set_used(std::int32_t)` would put the check back on every caller, at which point the private label is decoration. Note also that `remaining()` cannot underflow precisely because `consume()` is the only path that changes `used_`.

writing.section: Special member functions and the rules
writing.prompt: Write a `ScopedCounter` that increments a class-wide live count on construction and decrements it on destruction, with a static observer for the count. Then work through the suppression matrix in comments: state which special members the compiler still declares for this class given that you declared a destructor, and delete the ones that would corrupt the count.
checklist: The counter is an `inline static` data member initialized in the class
The observer is a `static` member function
The copy constructor and copy assignment are `= delete`
A comment states that declaring the destructor suppressed both implicit move operations
A comment states that the implicit copies would otherwise still be generated (deprecated, not removed), which is why they are deleted explicitly
writing.notes: Because the moves are already gone, a copy of this type would be the operation a container reaches for during relocation — which is the general shape of the "logging destructor" performance cliff. Deleting the copies makes the type honestly non-copyable instead of quietly wrong.

writing.section: Delegating and inherited constructors, statics, and ref-qualifiers
writing.prompt: Give an `Endpoint` two constructors: one taking host and port and validating that the port is in 1..65535, and one taking only a host and defaulting to port 443. Validation must appear exactly once in the class, and the single-argument constructor must not be usable as an implicit conversion.
checklist: The one-argument constructor delegates to the two-argument one in its member initializer list
The port check appears in exactly one constructor body
The one-argument constructor is `explicit`
The delegating constructor has no member initializers of its own besides the delegation
writing.notes: A delegating constructor may not also initialize members: the target constructor owns the whole initialization, and the delegating body can only add work afterwards. That restriction is what makes the pattern trustworthy — there is no path into the object that skips the validating constructor.

writing.section: Virtual destructors and deleting through base pointers
writing.prompt: Write the two base-class designs for a `Sink` callback interface: one that is registered but never owned through the base, where `delete sink;` on a base pointer must be a compile error; and one that is owned through the base and destroys the complete object correctly. State the rule in a comment on each.
checklist: The non-owning interface has a `protected`, non-virtual destructor
The owning interface has a `public virtual` destructor
Both interfaces declare the same pure virtual callback
Comments state which of the two allows `delete` through a base pointer
Neither design leaves a public non-virtual destructor on a polymorphic base
writing.notes: The third combination — public and non-virtual on a polymorphic base — is the one to recognize as a bug rather than a style choice: it compiles, it is undefined for every derived object deleted through the base, and nothing in the interface warns the caller.

writing.prompt: A slab allocator identifies a slot by a 20-bit epoch, a 10-bit index and a dirty flag. Write the packed `SlotId` bit-field struct with a compile-time check that it occupies exactly four bytes, and then write the equivalent `pack_slot`/`unpack_epoch` pair using explicit shifts and masks. Add a comment saying which of the two representations may be written to a file and why.
checklist: Every bit-field uses an explicitly unsigned base type
The widths sum to the size asserted, and a `static_assert` checks `sizeof`
The shift/mask version masks each field to its width before shifting it into place
The shifted results are combined into one unsigned value of the stated width
A comment states that bit-field allocation order is implementation-defined, so only the shift/mask form is safe for a wire or file format
writing.notes: A bit-field write is a read-modify-write of its whole storage unit: load, mask, merge, store. That is cheap for cold flags and expensive for a hot counter, and it also means adjacent bit-fields share one memory location for data-race purposes.

writing.section: Delegating and inherited constructors, statics, and ref-qualifiers
writing.prompt: A `Node` base has two constructors: one taking an id, one taking an id and a label. Write a derived `Leaf` that re-exposes both without retyping them and adds its own member with a default member initializer. Then add a commented-out `Leaf leaf{};` with a comment explaining why constructor inheritance does not give the derived class a default constructor.
checklist: `using Node::Node;` appears in the derived class
No constructor is written out by hand in `Leaf`
The derived member has a default member initializer so it is initialized on every inherited path
A comment states that inherited constructors do not include a default constructor and that the base has none to inherit
writing.notes: The default member initializer is doing real work: an inherited constructor initializes the base subobject only, so any derived member without an initializer would be left indeterminate on every one of those paths.

writing.prompt: Write `Celsius` and `Fahrenheit` value types over a `double` such that a bare number never becomes a temperature implicitly, a temperature never becomes a bare number implicitly, and converting between the two scales requires a named function. Add commented-out lines showing one initialization that is rejected and one that is accepted.
checklist: Both single-argument constructors are `explicit`
Any conversion back to `double` is an `explicit operator double()` or a named observer, never an implicit conversion operator
A free function converts one scale to the other and returns the target type
A commented-out copy-initialization from a `double` is shown as an error, alongside the accepted brace form
writing.notes: Without the two `explicit` keywords the pair is worse than a bare `double`: `to_fahrenheit(20.0)` would compile, and so would `celsius + fahrenheit` once both sides converted implicitly. The whole value of a units type is the conversions it refuses.

writing.prompt: A `Filter` base declares `virtual bool accept(int level) const`. A derived author wrote `bool accept(int level)` and is surprised that the base version still runs through a `Filter&`. Fix the derived declaration, add the keyword that would have turned the mistake into a compile error, and mark the derived class so that calls through its concrete type can be devirtualized.
checklist: The derived signature matches the base exactly, including the trailing `const`
`override` is present on the derived declaration and `virtual` is not repeated
The derived class is marked `final`
A commented-out line shows the non-const declaration and states that `override` rejects it
writing.notes: Without `override` the mismatched declaration is perfectly legal: it declares a *new*, non-virtual member that hides the base name for calls on a `ThresholdFilter` and is ignored for calls through a `Filter&`. That split behaviour is what makes the bug survive testing.

writing.section: Multiple inheritance, virtual inheritance, and RTTI
writing.prompt: A UI toolkit has `Widget` (holding an id), the interfaces `Drawable` and `Focusable`, and a `TextBox` that is both. Write the hierarchy so that a `TextBox` has exactly one `Widget` subobject and one id, and so that constructing a `TextBox` compiles. Add a comment stating which constructor actually initializes the shared base.
checklist: Both intermediate classes derive with `virtual` from `Widget`
`TextBox` names `Widget` directly in its own member initializer list
The intermediates also initialize `Widget`, for the case where one of them is the most-derived class
A comment states that the most-derived class initializes a virtual base and that the intermediates’ initializers are ignored when constructing a `TextBox`
A member of `TextBox` reads the id unqualified, showing that it is unambiguous
writing.notes: Drop the two `virtual` keywords and the same code fails twice over: `id()` becomes ambiguous, and `TextBox` may no longer name `Widget` in its initializer list because `Widget` is then not a direct or virtual base. The reason to know this is to recognize it in an existing hierarchy; new designs should reach for composition.

writing.prompt: Write a CRTP base `Chainable<Derived>` that accumulates steps through a `then(int)` member and reports their sum, but returns `Derived&` rather than `Chainable&` so a caller can keep chaining into derived-only members. Then write a `Pipeline` deriving from it with its own chainable member, and a call chain that mixes the two.
checklist: The base is a class template parameterized on the derived type
`then` returns `Derived&` via `static_cast<Derived&>(*this)`
`Pipeline` derives from `Chainable<Pipeline>`
A derived-only member is called after a base member in one chained expression
No virtual function appears anywhere
writing.notes: A non-template base returning `Chainable&` would compile and then break the chain: the next call would look up `name` in `Chainable`, which does not have it. Knowing the derived type at compile time is what keeps the return type precise — and it is the same mechanism, with the same cost, as CRTP used for static dispatch: one specialization of the base per derived class.
